tests.topic: A couple want a small wedding with forty guests; the bride's mother explains why that is impossible. For thirty years the family has attended, with a gift of money in an envelope, the weddings of relatives and neighbours who must now be invited in return. The daughter calls it a debt she never signed; the mother calls it belonging to a community.

Italy's industrial districts, such as the tile makers around Sassuolo: hundreds of small family firms in a few towns that compete and cooperate at once. The passage weighs the old claim that 'small is beautiful' (flexibility, skills handed down, trust between neighbours) against the limit that such firms rarely grow enough to fund research or face global rivals.

'Zero kilometre' food, bought from producers a short distance away, is promoted as the choice that respects the environment. The passage tests the idea: a tomato grown nearby in a heated greenhouse in winter can cost more energy than one that travelled by ship from a warm country. It concludes that distance is one measure among several, and that season counts for more.

In Italian schools a pupil with too many insufficient marks in June repeats the whole year, including the subjects passed. Defenders say a second chance at the same pace is better than moving on without the foundations; critics point out that those who repeat are the most likely to leave school altogether. The passage weighs the two cases and what each assumes about why a pupil fails.

In Italy the children of notaries, pharmacists and lawyers become notaries, pharmacists and lawyers far more often than chance would explain. The passage examines the reasons, from limited numbers of licences to a practice and clients already waiting, and the two readings of the fact: a family passing on knowledge, or a closed door for those born elsewhere.

When Italy banned smoking in bars, restaurants and offices in January 2005, among the first countries in Europe to do so, almost everyone predicted that Italians would ignore the rule. Within weeks it was respected nearly everywhere. The passage looks for the reasons: clear rules, fines for the owner and not only the smoker, and a majority that had been waiting for it.

In large Italian cities it can be hard to find a taxi on a rainy evening, because the number of licences has hardly changed in decades. A driver has often paid as much as a flat for a licence and counts on selling it to fund retirement. The passage explains why each new licence lowers the value of the old ones, and why the interest of passengers and the fairness owed to drivers pull apart.

A woman who was born in Venice and a shopkeeper who sells masks to visitors discuss an entry fee for day tourists. She says the city has fewer residents each year and is turning into a stage set; he says that without tourists there would be no work at all. They disagree on the fee but both fear a city where nobody lives.

The EUR district of Rome was designed in the late 1930s to celebrate the fascist regime, with white marble, bare arches and wide straight avenues. Today its buildings hold offices and museums and many architects admire them. The passage asks whether a building can be separated from the power that wanted it, and what a city should do with architecture of this kind.

Catenaccio, the 'door bolt', is the defensive football with which Italian teams won European cups in the 1960s: concede nothing, wait, and strike once. The passage sets admirers, who see intelligence and the art of making do with less, against critics, who see fear, and asks whether a way of playing can say something about a country.

Elena Ferrante, author of novels about two friends growing up in Naples that are read all over the world, has never shown her face: the name is a pseudonym and she answers questions only in writing. The passage discusses her argument that a finished book has no need of its author, and the curiosity of readers and journalists who refuse to accept it.

In 1954 the chemist Giulio Natta, in Milan, obtained a new plastic that was light, cheap and resistant to heat; it filled Italian homes with coloured buckets and basins and brought him the Nobel Prize in 1963. The passage follows how the very qualities that were celebrated then, above all that the material lasts and costs almost nothing, became the problem that is discussed today.

Como has been a silk city for centuries, though the mulberry trees and silkworms that once covered the countryside around it are gone and the raw thread now arrives from Asia. What remains is the knowledge of how to design, print and finish the cloth for the great fashion houses. The passage asks what a product owes to its place when the material comes from the other side of the world.

The chorus of the Hebrew slaves in Verdi's 'Nabucco' of 1842 is remembered as the secret anthem of Italians longing for a free and united country. Historians have found little sign that audiences of the time heard it that way: the legend seems to have grown after unification. The passage asks whether a symbol is any less true for having been built afterwards.

Two friends who have just graduated argue after one of them gets an interview thanks to a telephone call from his uncle. She calls it an unfair recommendation; he says his uncle only gave his name and he must still prove his worth. They try to find the line between knowing people, which happens everywhere, and taking the place of someone better.

When restorers cleaned the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1980 and 1994, centuries of candle smoke and glue came away and Michelangelo's dark, solemn figures appeared in bright pinks and greens. Some critics protested that the artist's own final shadows had been removed with the dirt. The passage uses the dispute to ask how anyone can know what an old painting looked like.

In 1516 Venice ordered its Jews to live on one small island of the city, whose gates were locked at night and guarded at the residents' own expense; the name of the place passed into many languages. Yet the same Venice let them stay and work when other states were expelling them. The passage examines an institution that was protection and segregation at once.

A bottle of tomato sauce can cost less than a euro in the supermarket; part of the reason is in the fields, where pickers recruited by illegal gang-masters are paid by the crate for ten hours in the sun. The passage follows the chain from field to shelf and asks who is responsible for the low price: the farmer, the retailer, or the customer who looks for the offer.

Several of Italy's best-known food companies, with factories on every continent, have never sold a single share on the stock exchange: the founding family owns everything. The passage weighs what this choice protects (long-term plans, secrecy, no pressure from quarterly results) against what it gives up (capital to grow, outside control), and asks whether it is prudence or distrust.

Many dishes sold as ancient tradition are surprisingly young: tiramisu appears in no cookbook before the 1960s and ciabatta bread was created by a miller in 1982. The passage argues that a tradition does not need to be old to be real, and asks why Italians defend recent recipes as if they were centuries old.

After his parents separate, an eleven-year-old spends one week in his mother's flat and one in his father's, with a bag that is always half packed. The arrangement was chosen because it is fair to both adults. The passage looks at it from the child's side and asks whether dividing time equally is the same thing as doing what is best for him.

An Italian woman back from five years in northern Europe tells an old friend that she now goes shopping in whatever she happens to be wearing. The friend replies that dressing with care is a form of respect for the people you meet; the first calls it fear of being judged. The dialogue circles the difference between elegance and conformity.

At Italian universities most examinations are oral, held in public and marked out of thirty, and a student who is unhappy with the mark may refuse it and try again weeks later. The passage explains how this works and weighs what it rewards (speaking clearly under pressure, the freedom to plan) against what it costs (years added to a degree, marks that depend on the examiner's mood).

Since 1978 Italy's national health service has treated everyone, rich or poor, largely free of charge. The passage sets this principle against everyday experience: an operation costs the patient nothing, but a specialist visit can mean months of waiting, so those who can afford it pay privately. It asks whether a right that arrives late is still equal for all.

On a small Italian island the ferry is the road to school, the hospital and the supermarket. In summer there are ten crossings a day for the tourists, in winter one, and none when the sea is rough. The passage follows the residents' argument that a connection which loses money is still a right, and the doubt about who should pay for it.

In many southern Italian towns houses stand without plaster, with steel rods sticking out of the flat roof: the family is waiting to add a floor when a son or daughter marries. The passage reads these unfinished houses as a way of saving in bricks rather than in a bank, and as the result of decades of building without permission and without a plan.

Every day in Italy an area of farmland as large as several football pitches disappears under warehouses, car parks and roads. The passage explains why this matters beyond the loss of fields: rain that the soil used to absorb now runs off the hard surface into rivers, and floods follow. It asks why a town council earns from new building and gains nothing from land left alone.

At the Rome Olympics of 1960 the marathon was run in the evening and ended by torchlight beside the Colosseum. It was won by an unknown Ethiopian soldier, Abebe Bikila, who ran barefoot and pulled away near an obelisk that Italy had carried off from his country during the occupation. The passage tells the race and what that victory, in that city, meant to those watching.

Two colleagues talk on the morning after the final of the Sanremo song festival. One says she did not watch it and then turns out to know every song and every dress; the other admits he saw all five evenings. They try to explain why a programme everybody calls old-fashioned is the one thing the whole country still watches together.

In a novel by Luigi Pirandello a man's life falls apart when his wife remarks that his nose leans slightly to one side: he realises that he has never seen himself as others see him, and that for each person he knows he is someone different. The passage explains the idea behind the story and asks whether it is a writer's paradox or an experience everyone has had.

In 1202 the merchant's son Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, explained to Europe the numerals he had learned in North Africa, with the zero that Roman figures lacked. A century later bankers in Florence were still forbidden to use them in their books, because a zero could too easily be altered into a six or a nine. The passage examines why a better tool can be resisted for good reasons as well as bad.

Artemisia Gentileschi, a painter of the seventeenth century and the first woman admitted to the academy of art in Florence, is often presented through the trial in which, at seventeen, she accused her teacher of rape. Her violent biblical heroines are then read as revenge. The passage asks whether this reading does her justice or reduces a professional artist, sought by courts across Europe, to one episode.

Between 1943 and 1945 the Italian Resistance fought German occupation, and also other Italians who had stayed with fascism. For decades the period was told only as a war of liberation; later some historians added the term civil war, and the phrase was contested. The passage explains why the choice of words matters and why both descriptions can be true at once.

The kiwi comes from China and took its name in New Zealand, yet since the 1970s Italy has become one of the largest producers in the world, starting from the plain south of Rome. The passage tells how farmers looking for a new crop made it local within one generation, and what the case suggests about 'typical' products: many arrived from elsewhere, some only earlier.

Supermarkets abroad are full of cheeses, sauces and cured meats with Italian-sounding names and a tricolour flag on the packet that were never made in Italy. Producers call it a theft worth billions; others answer that imitation is the price of success and that emigrants began many of these foods. The passage asks where homage ends and deception begins.

A bar owner and a regular customer argue when she wants to pay for a single coffee by card. He counts the commission on small payments and the wait at the till; she answers that cash is what makes undeclared income possible and that she no longer carries coins. Neither is wholly wrong, and they end with a compromise of his own invention.

Two teachers talk in the staff room in September. One has taught in the same school for twenty years; the other, on a one-year contract, is in her seventh school in seven years and learned where she would work four days ago. They discuss what this costs her, and what it costs classes that change their mathematics teacher every autumn.

In much of southern Italy the first son traditionally takes the name of his father's father and the first daughter that of her father's mother, so that four cousins may share one name. The passage follows a couple who want to choose freely and shows what is at stake on each side: a sign of continuity and respect, or a decision taken before the child's parents ever met.

A twenty-six-year-old graduate is on her third internship in three years, each one with real responsibilities and a reimbursement that does not cover the rent. The passage asks when training ends and cheap labour begins, and why both companies and young people keep accepting an arrangement that neither would defend in public.

After the earthquake of 1968 in western Sicily the town of Gibellina was not rebuilt on its ruins but some eighteen kilometres away, with wide streets and works by famous artists, while the old town was sealed under a vast field of white concrete that follows its lanes. The passage asks whether art can give an identity to a town, or whether the residents lost their home twice.

Wild boar now walk at night through the outskirts of Rome and other Italian cities, turning over rubbish bins. The passage traces the causes (abandoned fields, animals released in the past for hunting, waste left in the street) and the dispute between those who ask for culling and those who say the animals are only following the food that people leave them.

In the lectures he was preparing for an American university when he died in 1985, Italo Calvino named lightness as the first quality he wished for the literature of the future. The passage explains what he meant (taking weight away from stories and from sentences, as a bird is light and not as a feather is) and why he insisted that lightness is the opposite of superficiality.

For two thousand years it was believed that flies were born from rotting meat. In 1668 the Tuscan doctor Francesco Redi put meat into jars, left some open and covered others with gauze: maggots appeared only where flies could land. The passage explains why this simple comparison counts as one of the first modern experiments, and why an idea held for so long needed so little to fall.

A woman tells a friend of twenty years that she has started seeing a psychologist. The friend is almost offended: 'You have us for that.' The first explains the difference between being listened to with affection and being helped by someone trained; the second admits that in her family such things were never spoken about outside the house.

Renaissance cities such as Florence and Bologna passed laws on dress: how many pearls a woman could wear, how long a train could be, which fabrics were reserved for the nobility. Officials stopped women in the street, and the women found answers, calling a forbidden button a 'stud' because it had no buttonhole. The passage asks what the authorities were afraid of, and why such laws always failed.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the stars of Italian opera were singers who had been operated on as boys so that their voices would never break: a child's range with an adult's lungs. Audiences across Europe adored them and paid them fortunes; for each one who succeeded, many boys from poor families were harmed for nothing. The passage asks how to listen to a beauty that had this price.

In 1957 the architect Gio Ponti presented a wooden chair weighing 1.7 kilograms, light enough for a child to lift with one finger and strong enough to be thrown from a window in the factory's tests. He had started from an anonymous chair made for generations by craftsmen on the Ligurian coast and removed everything unnecessary. The passage asks whether design means inventing or improving.

School books give 476 as the year the Roman Empire in the West fell, when a general deposed a boy emperor and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. Few people living then noticed a turning point: laws, taxes, the Senate and daily life went on. The passage compares the idea of a fall with that of a slow transformation, and asks who needs history to have precise dates.

Whether shops should open on Sundays: shopping centres say customers who work all week have no other time, small shopkeepers say they cannot staff seven days and will lose to the large chains, and shop assistants ask when they are supposed to see their families. The passage shows that a question about opening hours is really one about what a day of rest is for.

Many elderly Italians are cared for at home by a live-in carer, often a woman from eastern Europe who has left her own children with their grandmother. The passage examines the double position she holds, almost one of the family and yet an employee, and the uncomfortable fact that one family stays together because another is divided.

A taxi driver and a passenger who cycles to work discuss a speed limit of thirty kilometres an hour on most streets of their city. He says his working day becomes longer and nobody respects the limit anyway; she quotes how much more likely a pedestrian is to survive a collision at thirty than at fifty. They agree only about the delivery vans.

Italian schools close for about thirteen weeks in summer, one of the longest breaks in Europe. The custom dates from a farming country that needed children in the fields, and from classrooms too hot in July. The passage sets teachers who defend the pause against working parents who must fill it and researchers who measure what pupils forget.

Since compulsory military service ended in 2005, young Italians can volunteer for a year of civil service in hospitals, libraries or associations, for a small monthly sum. The passage follows a volunteer in a centre for the elderly and asks whether the year is training in citizenship, a useful first experience of work, or a way of filling gaps in public services cheaply.

Until the middle of the twentieth century malaria was an Italian disease: it emptied the coastal plains, and in Sardinia it was part of ordinary life. Drained marshes, quinine and finally a huge insecticide campaign after the war removed it. The passage tells how, and reflects on how quickly a society forgets a danger once it has gone, and what that forgetting costs.

In 1857 work began on a railway tunnel more than thirteen kilometres long under the Alps between Italy and France, dug from both ends at once. With hand tools it would have taken a generation; the engineers counted on a compressed-air drill that was not yet ready when they started. The passage tells how the two teams met in 1870 almost exactly in line, and what the project says about betting on a technology still to come.

Corviale, on the edge of Rome, is a single block of public housing almost one kilometre long, designed in the 1970s to give thousands of people homes, shops and services under one roof. The services never opened and the building became a symbol of failure. The passage asks whether the idea was wrong or was simply abandoned halfway, and listens to residents who do not want to leave.

Many ski resorts in the Apennines and the lower Alps now depend on snow made by machines, which needs water, energy and cold nights that are becoming rarer. Valleys that live on winter tourism ask for public money for new lifts; others propose spending it on walking, cycling and food instead. The passage presents both and the fear behind the dispute: what a mountain village does without skiing.

Two parents watch their ten-year-old sons play football on a Saturday. One shouts instructions and protests at the referee, who is sixteen; the other finally asks him to stop. The first says he only wants his son to learn to win; the second reports that the boy has told his own son he would rather not play when his father is watching.

In 1954 an Italian expedition was the first to climb K2, and two men were photographed on the summit. The youngest member, Walter Bonatti, who had carried up their oxygen and been left to spend the night in the open above eight thousand metres, told a different story for fifty years before it was officially accepted. The passage asks what a national triumph is worth if it rests on a silence.

In the 1960s Italy, with a budget tiny beside those of the two superpowers, became one of the first countries to build and launch satellites of its own. An engineer, Luigi Broglio, had the launch base set on old oil platforms towed to the coast of Kenya, close to the equator, where the turning of the earth gives a rocket extra speed. The passage shows how a limit of means can produce an original idea.

In the late 1970s Giorgio Armani removed the padding and lining from the man's jacket so that it followed the body, and then offered the same soft jacket to women entering offices in large numbers. The passage argues that the change was more than a matter of taste: it raises the question of whether clothing gives authority or merely shows that it has already been won.

In August 1943 bombs destroyed the roof and auditorium of La Scala in Milan. In a city with thousands of homeless families the opera house was among the first buildings rebuilt, and it reopened in May 1946 with a concert conducted by Toscanini, back from exile. The passage asks why a ruined city chose a theatre before so much else, and whether the choice was a luxury or a need.

Some Italian churches that hold famous paintings now charge visitors for entry, while worshippers go in free by a side door. Supporters say that restoration and heating must be paid for and that crowds had made prayer impossible; opponents say that a church with a ticket office has become a museum. The passage asks whether the two uses of one building can live together.

For six centuries much of central Italy was farmed under a contract by which a peasant family lived on the landowner's farm and gave him half of everything it produced. The system was ended by law in the second half of the twentieth century. The passage holds two facts together: the contract kept families poor and dependent, and it also shaped the hills of mixed fields, vines and cypresses that visitors admire.

A fruit grower and the buyer for a supermarket chain discuss a load of peaches that are sweet but two millimetres below the size in the contract. She says customers pick with their eyes and leave the small ones on the shelf; he says a third of his harvest stays on the ground for reasons unrelated to taste. They look for someone to blame and find a chain of choices.

World demand for hazelnut spreads and chocolates has led whole districts of central and northern Italy to replace mixed fields, vines and woods with rows of hazel trees. Farmers at last have a crop that pays; neighbours point to a single-crop landscape, more chemical treatments and a lake that is suffering. The passage asks how much specialisation a territory can bear.

Adriano Olivetti's typewriter factory in Ivrea in the 1950s: wages above the average, a nursery, a library and glass walls so workers could see the mountains. The passage asks whether this was the idealism of one unusual man or simply good business, and why so few companies copied a model that made excellent profits.

The tomato reached Italy from the Americas in the sixteenth century and was grown for a long time as a curiosity that many believed harmful; almost three centuries passed before it was regularly cooked with pasta. The passage describes what Italians ate before it and uses the story to question the idea of an unchanging national cuisine.

In Italian couples where both partners have a job, women still spend far more hours a day than men on cooking, cleaning and care, one of the widest gaps in Europe. The passage compares a couple in their sixties with their son and his partner, and asks whether the change between generations is real or whether men have simply learned to 'help' with work that remains hers.

In 1945, in a village near Reggio Emilia, parents sold a tank, some lorries and horses left behind by the retreating army and used the money to build a nursery school with their own hands. From it grew an approach, studied today by educators from all over the world, that treats small children as researchers. The passage asks why a method born from poverty is now copied by wealthy schools.

For decades Italian factories, offices and shops have closed together for two or three weeks around the fifteenth of August. The passage explains where the habit came from, when whole production lines had to stop at once, and asks whether a collective holiday still makes sense when it means crowded beaches, high prices and cities where nothing is open.

Two friends at the counter notice that the espresso has gone up by twenty cents. One says the low, almost fixed price of a coffee is a social pact that lets anyone enter a bar; the other, whose sister runs a bar, lists rent, energy and staff and says the pact is paid for by the people who work behind the counter.

In a bookshop a customer confesses, almost apologising, that he reads only crime novels, called 'gialli' in Italy after the yellow covers of a series first published in 1929. The bookseller answers that the best ones describe a city, its offices and its injustices better than many prize-winning novels. They discuss who decides what counts as literature.

The short sleep after lunch was once normal in Italy, above all in the south, where shops closed through the hottest hours. Offices with a one-hour break have almost ended it, just as studies suggest that twenty minutes of rest improve attention in the afternoon. The passage asks whether the habit was laziness, as visitors used to think, or good sense.

Italy has thousands of kilometres of railway lines closed since the 1950s, when buses and cars made small branch lines unprofitable. Some valleys want the old track turned into a cycle path; others want the trains back, at least for tourists at weekends. The passage compares the two projects and what each one decides about the future of the villages along the line.

In Milan two residential towers carry hundreds of trees and thousands of shrubs on their balconies, watered by a central system and pruned by gardeners who work hanging from ropes. Admirers see a model for cities that need shade and clean air; critics note the cost of the flats and of the upkeep. The passage asks whether it is a solution or an expensive symbol.

Taranto, in the south, lives beside one of the largest steelworks in Europe: it gives work to thousands of families and covers the nearest district in red dust that has been linked to illness. The passage presents the choice the city has faced for decades, work or health, and asks why a community should ever be made to choose between the two.

In Italian towns, before dinner, people of every age walk slowly up and down the main street with no destination, greeting and observing one another. The passage describes this evening walk as an unwritten institution with rules of its own, and asks what a town loses when the walk moves to a shopping centre outside it.

Surveys say that more than half of Italians do not read a single book in a year, and yet the country publishes tens of thousands of new titles and fills the squares of Mantua every September for a literature festival. The passage examines the paradox: a small group of strong readers buys most of the books, and listening to an author is not the same as reading one.

A resident of a public housing block talks with the artist the council has paid to paint a mural six floors high on its blank wall. He says that nobody asked the people who live there and that the stairs still need repair; she says colour brings visitors and attention to a forgotten district. They discuss who street art is for once it is commissioned.

A few days before the earthquake that struck L'Aquila in 2009, a commission of experts met in the city after months of small tremors, and the public heard a reassuring message. Seven members were later tried, and most were acquitted on appeal. The passage clarifies the charge, which was not failing to predict an earthquake but how the risk had been communicated, and asks what scientists can honestly promise.

The Italian films of the years after the war that changed world cinema were shot in real streets, with a factory worker or a fisherman in the leading part. The passage explains that this was at first necessity, since the studios outside Rome were housing refugees and money was short, and discusses how a lack of means turned into a style that directors later chose on purpose.

In the year 212 the emperor Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to nearly every free inhabitant of the empire, from Britain to Egypt. Ancient writers suspected that he wanted more people to pay the taxes owed by citizens; modern readers have seen a remarkably open idea of belonging. The passage weighs the two readings and asks whether the motive changes the value of the act.

In many Italian vineyards the grape harvest now begins two or three weeks earlier than it did forty years ago, and growers are planting higher up the hills in search of cool nights. The passage explains the difficulty this creates: the rules that protect a famous wine tie it to precise slopes and grape varieties, fixed when the climate was different.
